ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: CNS pathology covers diseases of the brain, spinal cord, and meninges. Diagnosis blends clinical clues with imaging and CSF studies. Management targets the underlying cause and supports neurological function.

sections.p: CNS pathology refers to any structural or functional disease affecting the brain, spinal cord, or meninges. Diagnosis starts with history, exam, imaging (CT/MRI), and CSF analysis when indicated.
b: CNS disease = brain, spinal cord, meninges

t.b: Detects tumors, demyelination, infarcts, infections; shows lesion location and characteristics.
Rapid assessment of hemorrhage, mass effect, and acute stroke.
Evaluates CSF for infection, inflammation, or malignancy; checks opening pressure, cell count, protein, glucose.
Assesses seizure activity and diffuse encephalopathy.
Identifies cognitive deficits and helps localize lesions.

sections.p: Severity is graded by neurological deficit, imaging findings, and functional status. Staging systems exist for specific diseases (e.g., WHO grade for gliomas, NIH Stroke Scale for stroke).
Causes vary by age and setting. In low‑resource areas, infections dominate; in high‑income settings, neoplasia and autoimmune disease are common.
b: Trauma: spinal cord injury, traumatic brain injury

sections.p: Symptoms depend on lesion location. Common presentations include focal deficits, altered consciousness, seizures, headache, and cranial nerve palsies.
b: Cranial nerve palsies (e.g., facial weakness, visual loss)

sections.p: Select tests based on clinical suspicion and resource availability. When a test is unavailable, clinical judgment and basic imaging guide management.

t.b: Identifies lesion type and extent; essential for tumors and demyelination.
First line for suspected hemorrhage or acute stroke when MRI is unavailable.
CSF analysis for infection or inflammatory markers; avoid if increased ICP suspected.
Screen for infection or inflammatory disease.
Detects infectious causes common in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Urgent signs include sudden severe headache, loss of consciousness, focal neurological decline, or signs of increased intracranial pressure. Complications can be fatal if untreated.
Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care. Drug choices consider efficacy, safety, and resource constraints.
b: Supportive care: airway, breathing, circulation, ICP monitoring

sections.p: Regular monitoring of neurological status, imaging, and CSF when indicated. Prevention focuses on vaccination, infection control, and early treatment of risk factors.
Several conditions mimic CNS pathology; distinguishing features guide diagnosis.
b: Infectious meningitis vs. viral encephalitis (fever, neck stiffness vs. altered mental status)

sections.p: Some tests may give false negatives or positives; clinical correlation is essential.
b: Serology can be delayed; PCR preferred for viral infections

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of increased intracranial pressure (papilledema, vomiting)

faq.q: What is the most common CNS infection in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: Tuberculous meningitis is the most frequent and deadly CNS infection in many low‑resource regions.

faq.q: How do I differentiate bacterial from viral meningitis clinically?
faq.a: Bacterial meningitis presents with fever, neck stiffness, and rapid deterioration; viral meningitis often has milder symptoms and better prognosis.

faq.q: When is a lumbar puncture contraindicated?
faq.a: It is contraindicated if there is suspected increased intracranial pressure, focal brain lesion, or coagulopathy.
